Is premature optimization the root of all evil? Casey Muratori, @cmuratori, programmer and performance nerd, with three takeaways:

#1 - Performance experts can't clean up after the fact

“The idea is I'm just going to delay optimization work. I'm just going to make whatever I'm going to make and clean up the mess later.

You call in some performance experts and they go, "There's nothing we could do for you. Sorry." 

Why? Because you created a serial dependency chain. All of your code looks like: wait for a network request to come back, do something. Wait for a network request to come back, do something. And that serial dependency chain can't really be shortened without just rewriting it."

#2 - Engineering teams must think about performance upfront  

"At the top of every operation, you need to figure out all the things you might want to ask a server for, ask for all of those things and then you do all of your processing there. You only create a chain of dependencies if you absolutely couldn't have determined what it was you needed to ask a server for."

#3 - Hotspot code bases are designed, not a given 

"You have to engineer upfront for a hotspot code base that people can then optimize. The crucial takeaway is everybody on your team who is making architectural decisions, those people must know performance. They must make decisions that will allow the other people downstream of them to use an architecture which can be optimized later.

If you don't do that, you're just rolling the dice.”

quotedPost.text:
Today's Pragmatic Engineer newsletter [https://t.co/mxzBi1O6ns] was talking about Meta's misguided attempt to fire everybody and replace them with AI. Zuch was evididently thinking (if you can call it that) that mass layoffs would make them look more like a startup.

The attached image👇 is instructive. Meta is on the left and a typical startup is on the right. That smaller team is presented as "AI Native," but the fact is that most effective software organizations, not just startups, have had that small-team structure long before AI was on the scene. It's just a more effective way to work. 

10-20 person teams is insanely large—the communication overhead enough will kill you, and many of the roles have a large bureaucratic component that doesn't help one iota in geting software out the door. On the smaller teams, people have flexible roles and everybody is entirely focused on getting a product out the door rather than bureaucracy. It's—dare I say it—agile. And, yes, it will work much better. That's not because of AI, though, it's because of the flexibility and the focus. AI is just a tool that team can use to be more effective. It does not replace people. 

Thinking you can make a large team more effective by firing half the team reminds me of the thinking—popular years ago—that if you bought lots of books, your kids would somehow become smarter, through osmosis I guess. The thinking confuses corelation (smart kids come from homes with lots of books) with causation (the mere presense of books makes kids smarter). It's not the decorating decision, of course, it's the parents who are reading the books that are the key factor.

If you fire half the team without getting rid of the bureaucracy and ineffective ways of working those people supported, you'll just burn out whoever's left. That's exactly what happened at Meta.

It's not the size of the team that makes it better; rather, effective teams don't carry the overhead and bad ways of working, so are naturally smaller. Start by fixing the way you work. The team size will take care of itself.

Three interesting things we talked about:

1. Is performance starting to matter to businesses?

Enterprise software buyers care mainly about cost, compliance, and capabilities – but not performance. Even so, there are some products gaining major popularity and market share due to their performance, such as File Pilot (next-gen file explorer) and the Blick video editor. Is the tide turning?

2. Profiler-driven performance optimization is the wrong way to optimize

The standard way of optimizing is to profile the application, tweak hotspots, then check if the stats have improved. But this only finds a local minimum; Casey says every engineer he’s worked with who was a great “optimizer” began by establishing what the hardware could theoretically do, and then did not stop until they’d closed the gap to that performance level.

3. Take a grain of salt with conventional wisdom that premature optimization is the “root of all evil”

Many devs use it as an excuse to delay performance optimization, but Casey says that not optimizing in time could mean that only performance hotspots can be fixed later, and not the architectural issues that create poor performance. Architect your system to be performant, or you’ll have trouble solving problems without a rewrite!

Months back, I started to do something new that I didn't tell anyone: at the end of each podcast, think back to what I found very memorable about my time with the guest. And close the podcast with this.

Honestly, I mostly did it for myself. If I spent closer to two hours talking with a person, I wanted to collect my thoughts, and then why not close with these?

And despite being lucky enough to have plenty of folks listening: it took more than six months to get any feedback on this change. Thankfully, it was a positive one - phew!

I figured this would be a helpful addition (the very worst case a neutral one) - and it once again shows that you can't rely only on feedback; often, you just do what feels right.

Asana says OpenAI Codex completed an engineering migration it had expected to take at least five years in about two weeks, for roughly $12,000 in model and infrastructure costs.

The project: removing Enzyme, an outdated testing system that had become a blocker to upgrading Asana’s frontend stack. The company’s previous staffing plan estimated the migration would cost roughly $6 million.

Instead, Asana gave Codex a prompt only five sentences long.

Up to four coding agents worked in parallel, each operating in a separate copy of the codebase. A human engineer checked progress roughly twice per day and reviewed every proposed change before approval. Asana says simpler instructions actually worked better than a more elaborate setup.

The result:

Expected timeline: ≥5 years
Actual: 1.5 weeks of engineering effort across 2 calendar weeks
Previous staffing estimate: ~$6M
Model + infrastructure cost: ~$12K

There are probably THOUSANDS of old migrations and rewrites sitting inside companies because nobody can justify spending years on them.

If agents make those projects cheap enough to attempt the engineering backlog itself starts changing.

1. The question engineers need to answer: what would it take for you to be fully comfortable shipping code you have not read?

Charity believes it is a “when” and not an “if” that professional software engineers will ship code they never looked at – and thus do not understand – to production. Engineering is building the systems that validate this code, and allow shipping with full confidence.

2.  AI could have the software industry go through the “pets” to “cattle” change that compute infra went through in the 2010s. 

Up to now, writing software from scratch was far more expensive than editing existing software. But now, generating hundreds of variants of a function can be done faster than how long it would take you to hand-write it once.

Charity believes that we might be at the beginning of the transition from “pets” to “cattle” that happened at the hardware infrastructure layer. Before the 2010s, configuring and repairing individual servers was commonly done. But with tools like Terraform and Kubernetes, individual servers having issues are no longer fixed up: they are re-created instead. Charity thinks the same might happen with code, sooner rather than later. When there’s an issue with the code, generate new code that solves it, and is verifyably correct.​

3. Non-deterministic systems require more engineering discipline versus before. 

With code written by AI, we’re reducing the trust in the code (because we no longer wrote it), so we need to increase trust at the other part of the development process. Specifically, at validation: with things like tests, evals, and conformance testing.
